hints: Focus on what must happen first before silver nitrate can do anything, the halogen has to leave the carbon as a halide ion.
Compare the carbon-halogen bonds present, the C-I bond is much weaker and longer than C-Br, C-Cl and C-F.
Look for the molecule that contains the most easily broken C-X bond, as that will release its ion fastest on warming with water.
walkthrough:
**Understand the test**

Warming a halogenoalkane with water hydrolyses it and releases a halide ion. That ion then forms the precipitate.

$$\text{R-X + H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{R-OH + X}^- + \text{H}^+$$
$$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{X}^- \rightarrow \text{AgX(s)}$$

**Decide what controls speed**

All the halogens here are on primary $\text{CH}_2\text{X}$ groups, so the structure type is the same. The rate therefore depends on C-X bond strength.

Bond strength increases in the order: $$\text{C-I < C-Br < C-Cl < C-F}$$

**Compare the four compounds**

Compound A has only $\text{C-Cl}$ bonds. Compound B has $\text{C-Cl}$ and $\text{C-F}$ bonds. Compound D has $\text{C-Br}$, $\text{C-Cl}$ and $\text{C-F}$ bonds.

Only one compound contains the very weak $\text{C-I}$ bond, so its $\text{I}^-$ is released quickest and gives $\text{AgI}$ precipitate fastest.

options.A: Contains only three C-Cl bonds. Chloride is released by hydrolysis, but C-Cl is stronger than C-Br and C-I, so precipitation is slower than for compounds containing Br or I.
options.B: Contains C-Cl and C-F bonds. C-F is very strong and hardly hydrolyses, so reaction relies on the one C-Cl bond. This is slower than hydrolysis of C-Br or C-I.
options.C: Contains C-F bonds and one C-I bond. The C-I bond is the longest and weakest, so it hydrolyses most readily on warming to give I- ions, which quickly form yellow AgI precipitate with Ag+.
options.D: Contains C-Br, C-Cl and C-F bonds. Bromide is released faster than chloride, so this is faster than A and B, but C-Br is still stronger than C-I, so it is slower than the iodine-containing compound.
